title: Heart Structure, Layers and Chambers
body:
## What it is
The heart is a hollow muscular pump (about 300 g) sitting in the mediastinum between the lungs, resting on the diaphragm. It delivers oxygen and nutrients to tissues by pumping blood.

## Must-know facts
- Three wall layers, inside to outside:
  - Endocardium: lines the chambers and valves.
  - Myocardium: the muscle layer that actually contracts.
  - Epicardium: the outermost layer; the main coronary arteries run on it.
- The pericardium is a fibrous sac with a thin film of lubricating fluid. Its visceral layer hugs the epicardium; the parietal layer anchors the heart in the mediastinum. Fluid or scarring here causes [[Pericarditis and Pericardiocentesis]] and [[Cardiac Tamponade]].
- Atria (upper) are the receiving chambers; ventricles (lower) are the pumping chambers.
- Systole = contraction; diastole = relaxation and ventricular filling. Pumping is a rhythmic cycle of the two.
- The apical impulse (point of maximal impulse) is felt over the apex at the left mid-clavicular line, normally in the 5th intercostal space.

## How the exam asks about it
- "Which layer contracts?" (myocardium) or "which layer is inflamed in endocarditis / myocarditis / pericarditis?" Match the suffix to the layer: endo = inner, myo = muscle, peri = sac.
- Auscultation and pulse-point questions usually build on landmarks, so know where the apex sits.

## Related topics
[[Cardiac Output, Preload, Afterload and Contractility]], [[Heart Sounds S1 to S4]], [[Cardiac Conduction System and Autonomic Control]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout says the apical impulse is at the "15th" intercostal space. That is a typo; the adult apex is at the 5th ICS, left mid-clavicular line.

title: Cardiac Output, Preload, Afterload and Contractility
body:
## What it is
Cardiac output (CO) is the volume of blood the heart ejects each minute, about 5 L/min at rest.
- CO = heart rate (HR) x stroke volume (SV).
- Normal heart rate is 60 to 100 beats per minute, controlled by the autonomic nervous system.
- Stroke volume is the blood ejected by the left ventricle per beat.

## The three determinants of stroke volume
- Preload: how stretched the ventricle is at the end of diastole, set by the blood returning to the heart. Starling's law: the more the heart fills, the more forcefully it contracts, so higher preload gives higher SV (up to a limit).
- Contractility: the force of muscle contraction. Raised by catecholamines, sympathetic activity and positive inotropes (the "3 D's": digoxin, dopamine, dobutamine). Higher contractility gives higher SV.
- Afterload: the resistance the ventricle must push against to open the semilunar valves. It rises with high blood pressure and narrowed vessels. Higher afterload gives LOWER SV.

## Why it matters for nursing
- Heart failure, shock and many cardiac drugs are all explained by moving one of these levers. Diuretics and nitrates lower preload; ACE inhibitors and vasodilators lower afterload; digoxin raises contractility.
- Low CO means poor perfusion: watch for hypotension, weak pulses, cool skin, low urine output, confusion.

## How the exam asks about it
- "Which drug reduces afterload?" or "which change would lower stroke volume?" Remember: preload and contractility go with SV, afterload goes against it.

## Related topics
[[Heart Failure: Types, Causes and Compensation]], [[Drugs Used in Heart Failure]], [[Heart Structure, Layers and Chambers]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout says that in exercise cardiac output rises fourfold "to 2 L/min". That cannot be right (a four-fold rise from 5 L/min is about 20 L/min). Verify the figure.

title: Heart Sounds S1 to S4
body:
## What it is
Heart sounds come from valve closure and from blood hitting the ventricular walls.

## Must-know facts
- S1 ("lub"): closure of the atrioventricular (mitral and tricuspid) valves; loudest at the apex. Marks the start of systole.
- S2 ("dub"): closure of the semilunar (aortic and pulmonic) valves; loudest at the base.
- S3 ("ventricular gallop"): heard early in diastole when the ventricle is stiff or overloaded, as in heart failure or valve regurgitation. It can be normal in people younger than about 30.
- S4: heard in late diastole with atrial contraction against a stiff, resistant ventricle (hypertrophy, injury to the ventricular wall). Considered abnormal.

## Why it matters
- A new S3 in a client with dyspnea and crackles supports [[Left-Sided versus Right-Sided Heart Failure]]. An S3 or S4 can also appear in [[Myocardial Infarction: Presentation and Cardiac Markers]].
- Murmurs (turbulent flow through narrowed or leaky valves) are covered in [[Valvular Heart Disease: Overview and Mitral Stenosis]].

## How the exam asks about it
- Location questions: apex = S1, base = S2.
- "A new S3 in a middle-aged client with orthopnea suggests what?" Heart failure.

## Memory aid (made up here)
S3 = "Slosh" (fluid overload), S4 = "Stiff" ventricle.

title: Cardiac Conduction System and Autonomic Control
body:
## What it is
The heart makes and spreads its own electrical impulse. Three properties: automaticity (starts an impulse itself), excitability (responds to one) and conductivity (passes it on).

## The pathway and the built-in rates
- SA node (junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium): the natural pacemaker, 60 to 100 bpm.
- AV node (near the interatrial septum): briefly delays the impulse so the ventricles can fill; its own rate is 40 to 60 bpm.
- Bundle of His, then right and left bundle branches in the interventricular septum.
- Purkinje fibers in the ventricular walls: cause ventricular contraction; their own rate is 20 to 40 bpm. They act as the last-resort backup pacemaker.
- Rule: if a higher pacemaker fails, the next one down takes over at a slower rate.

## Autonomic control
- Parasympathetic impulses via the vagus nerve slow the rate; sympathetic impulses speed it up.
- Baroreceptors in the aortic arch and both internal carotid arteries sense blood pressure. When pressure falls, less baroreceptor signalling reduces vagal inhibition of the SA node, so sympathetic activity rises: vasoconstriction and a faster heart rate bring pressure back up.

## How the exam asks about it
- "Which structure is the normal pacemaker?" or "what happens to the rate when the SA node fails?" (AV junction takes over at 40 to 60.)
- Low BP with a fast pulse is the baroreceptor response, a clue to early shock ([[Circulatory Shock: Hypovolemic and Cardiogenic]]).

## Related topics
[[ECG Waves and Intervals]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout says the AV delay is "0.8 milliseconds"; the usual figure is about 0.08 to 0.12 second (that is the PR interval portion). It also lists the AV node's location loosely; confirm.

title: ECG Waves and Intervals
body:
## What it is
The ECG records the heart's electrical activity as waves. Learn what each part means and its normal size.

## Must-know facts
- P wave: atrial depolarization. Small and rounded, no wider than 0.12 second.
- QRS complex: ventricular depolarization (atrial repolarization is hidden within it). Normal width 0.04 to 0.10 second.
- T wave: ventricular repolarization. Tall T waves (over about 5 mm in limb leads) are abnormal.
- PR interval: start of P to start of QRS; the time for the impulse to cross atria, AV junction and Purkinje system. Normal 0.12 to 0.20 second.
- QT interval: total ventricular depolarization plus repolarization, roughly 0.32 to 0.40 second. A prolonged QT raises the risk of torsades de pointes, a lethal ventricular dysrhythmia.
- PP interval gives the atrial rate and rhythm; RR interval gives the ventricular rate and rhythm.
- U wave: may reflect Purkinje repolarization; seen mainly when potassium is low (hypokalemia).

## Link to disease
- ST elevation, abnormal Q waves and T-wave inversion point to infarction: [[Myocardial Infarction: Presentation and Cardiac Markers]].
- ST depression and T inversion suggest ischemia: [[Angina Pectoris: Types, Triggers and Findings]].
- Low-voltage QRS, ST elevation or heart block can appear in [[Myocarditis]].

## How the exam asks about it
- "Which wave represents ventricular repolarization?" and "a U wave suggests which electrolyte problem?"

## Related topics
[[Cardiac Conduction System and Autonomic Control]]

## Check against your textbook
- Normal QT varies with heart rate; the handout's single range is a simplification.

title: Coronary Artery Disease and Atherosclerosis
body:
## What it is
Coronary artery disease (CAD) is the most common cardiovascular disease in adults. Its usual cause is atherosclerosis: fatty plaque building up in the artery wall. (Arteriosclerosis is the general term for thickened, hardened arteries; atherosclerosis is the fatty-plaque type.) It also drives stroke (CVA). When the narrowed lumen cannot meet the heart's demand, the cells become ischemic.

## Risk factors
- Modifiable: hyperlipidemia, smoking and tobacco, hypertension, diabetes, metabolic syndrome, obesity, physical inactivity.
- Non-modifiable: family history (a first-degree relative with heart disease before 55 in men or 65 in women), increasing age (over 45 men, over 55 women), male sex, and race.

## Findings
- May be silent for years. Then: chest pain, palpitations, dyspnea, syncope, marked fatigue.

## Treatment
- Procedures: PTCA (balloon compresses plaque and widens the vessel), laser angioplasty (vaporizes plaque), atherectomy (removes plaque), stent (keeps the vessel open, reduces re-narrowing), CABG (bypass graft around the blockage).
- Drugs: nitrates (dilate coronary arteries, lower preload and afterload), calcium channel blockers (dilate, reduce spasm), cholesterol-lowering drugs, beta-blockers.

## Nursing focus
Teach risk-factor control: stop smoking, manage BP and glucose, lose weight, exercise. See [[Lipid Profile and Heart-Healthy Diet]] and [[Angina Pectoris: Types, Triggers and Findings]].

## How the exam asks about it
- Which risk factor can the client change? Stopping smoking is usually the strongest teaching answer. Also see [[Stop Smoking and Tobacco Cessation]].

## Related topics
[[Angina Treatment: Procedures and Drugs]], [[Myocardial Infarction: Management and Drug Therapy]]

title: Lipid Profile and Heart-Healthy Diet
body:
## What it is
The fasting lipid profile (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides) measures cardiac risk. All adults 20 and older should have one at least every 5 years, more often if abnormal.

## Handout values
- Total cholesterol: 140 to 199 mg/dL
- LDL: lower than 130 mg/dL
- HDL: 30 to 70 mg/dL
- Triglycerides: lower than 200 mg/dL

## Must-know facts
- LDL is the "bad" carrier that deposits cholesterol in vessel walls. High total cholesterol, high LDL and high triglycerides raise CAD risk.
- HDL is "good": it carries lipoproteins such as LDL to the liver for breakdown and excretion, so a high HDL is protective.
- Cholesterol is found in all tissues, in nerve and brain cells and cell membranes, and in some gallstones.

## Diet teaching
- Low calorie, low sodium, low cholesterol, low fat, with more dietary fiber.
- A Mediterranean-style pattern (vegetables, fish, limited red meat) is reported to lower cardiovascular deaths.

## How the exam asks about it
- Pick the meal choice that fits a client with high LDL; or which lab result is protective (high HDL).

## Related topics
[[Coronary Artery Disease and Atherosclerosis]], [[Hypertension: Classification and Risk Factors]], [[Nutrition]]

## Check against your textbook
- Reference ranges differ between sources and labs (especially LDL targets and HDL lower limits). Use your textbook's values.

title: Heart Failure: Types, Causes and Compensation
body:
## What it is
Heart failure (HF) is the heart's inability to pump enough blood to meet tissue needs for oxygen and nutrients. The dominant problem is poor tissue perfusion from low cardiac output.

## Causes
Hypertension, CAD, cardiomyopathy, substance abuse (alcohol, cocaine, amphetamines), valve disease, previous MI, congenital defects, cardiac infection or inflammation, and high-output (hyperkinetic) states.

## Types
- Systolic HF: weakened muscle that cannot contract well.
- Diastolic HF: stiff, non-compliant muscle that cannot fill well.
- Symptoms depend on which ventricle fails: see [[Left-Sided versus Right-Sided Heart Failure]].

## ACC/AHA stages
- A: high risk, no structural disease, no symptoms.
- B: structural disease or LV dysfunction, still no symptoms.
- C: structural disease with current or past symptoms.
- D: refractory end-stage disease needing specialized treatment.

## Compensation (and why it backfires)
- Sympathetic stimulation: faster heart rate, stronger beat, but arterial vasoconstriction raises afterload and workload.
- Renin-angiotensin system: low renal perfusion releases renin, making angiotensin I, which ACE (in the lungs) converts to angiotensin II, a strong vasoconstrictor. Angiotensin II also triggers aldosterone (sodium and water retention) and ADH. Result: fluid overload. This is why ACE inhibitors and diuretics help ([[Drugs Used in Heart Failure]]).

## How the exam asks about it
- Explain why daily weights and sodium limits matter, or which drug blocks which step of the cascade.

## Related topics
[[Cardiac Output, Preload, Afterload and Contractility]], [[Cardiomyopathies: Dilated, Hypertrophic and Restrictive]]
outlineRefs: TWO MAJOR TYPES OF HEART FAILURE

title: Left-Sided versus Right-Sided Heart Failure
body:
## What it is
Left HF backs blood into the lungs; right HF backs blood into the body. Quick rule from the handout: Left = Lung.

## Left-sided findings
- Pulmonary congestion: dyspnea, cough, crackles, low oxygen saturation, orthopnea.
- Frothy, pink, blood-tinged sputum signals pulmonary edema (an emergency).
- An S3 "ventricular gallop" may be heard.

## Right-sided findings
- Jugular vein distention, dependent edema (feet, or sacrum if bed-bound), hepatomegaly, ascites, weight gain from fluid.
- Left failure is the most common cause of right failure; sustained pulmonary hypertension also causes it.

## Priority nursing actions (reasoning: breathing and oxygenation first)
1. Sit the client upright (semi-Fowler's or higher; some prefer a chair), give oxygen as ordered to ease work of breathing.
2. Monitor vital signs, cardiac rhythm and breath sounds.
3. Give diuretics as prescribed; record intake and output.
4. Weigh daily, same scale and time, to catch fluid gain early.
5. For right HF: assess edema, measure abdominal girth, avoid unnecessary IV fluids.
6. Teach low-sodium eating.

## Common nursing diagnoses
Impaired gas exchange, decreased cardiac output, activity intolerance, and risk for pulmonary edema, pneumonia and dysrhythmias.

## How the exam asks about it
- "Which finding needs action first?" Pink frothy sputum or worsening dyspnea outranks edema (Maslow: oxygenation).

## Related topics
[[Heart Failure: Types, Causes and Compensation]], [[Drugs Used in Heart Failure]], [[Heart Sounds S1 to S4]]

title: Drugs Used in Heart Failure
body:
## What it is
Heart failure drugs work on volume, afterload, heart rate and contractility.

## Drug groups from the handout
- Diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide, metolazone, hydrochlorothiazide, spironolactone): reduce blood volume and relieve symptoms. Watch for potassium changes; most waste potassium, spironolactone keeps it.
- ACE inhibitors (captopril, enalapril, lisinopril): lower afterload.
- Beta-blockers (metoprolol, atenolol, carvedilol): help raise ejection fraction and reduce ventricular size.
- Inotrope (digoxin): strengthens contraction.
- Vasodilators (nitroprusside, nitroglycerin ointment): lower preload and ease dyspnea.

## Nursing points
- Check potassium before and during diuretic or digoxin therapy; low potassium raises digoxin toxicity risk.
- Take apical pulse before digoxin and hold and report if it is below the ordered threshold or if toxicity signs appear (see [[Myocarditis]] for the toxicity picture).
- Monitor BP before ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers.
- Pair drugs with daily weights and sodium restriction.

## How the exam asks about it
- Match drug to purpose (digoxin = contractility, ACE inhibitor = afterload, diuretic = volume, nitrate = preload).

## Related topics
[[Heart Failure: Types, Causes and Compensation]], [[Left-Sided versus Right-Sided Heart Failure]], [[Essential Drugs]]

## Check against your textbook
- Specific dosing and hold parameters are not in the handout. Use your pharmacology text.

title: Valvular Heart Disease: Overview and Mitral Stenosis
body:
## What it is
Valve disease means a valve does not open fully (stenosis) or does not close fully, letting blood leak back (insufficiency / regurgitation). Types: mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse, aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation.

## Mitral stenosis
- Usually follows rheumatic endocarditis: fibrosis and calcification thicken and narrow the valve.
- Blood cannot leave the left atrium easily, so left atrial pressure rises and the atrium dilates; pressure backs up to the pulmonary artery and may eventually cause right-sided failure.

## Findings
- Low-pitched, rumbling diastolic murmur at the apex.
- Dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (sudden breathlessness during sleep), dry cough, hemoptysis, pulmonary edema, atrial dysrhythmias.

## Treatment
- Anticoagulants to prevent atrial clots.
- Valvuloplasty (including percutaneous balloon type) or mitral valve replacement.

## Priority nursing actions
- Position high Fowler's to ease breathing.
- Monitor for pulmonary edema, thrombus/embolism, arrhythmias (palpitations, anxiety), ABGs, and daily weight.
- Teach symptoms to report; low-sodium, low-fat diet.

## How the exam asks about it
- Identify murmur timing: diastolic rumble at apex = mitral stenosis. Also expect rheumatic fever history.

## Related topics
[[Mitral Regurgitation and Mitral Valve Prolapse]], [[Aortic Regurgitation]], [[Aortic Stenosis]], [[Infective Endocarditis]]

title: Mitral Regurgitation and Mitral Valve Prolapse
body:
## What it is
- Mitral regurgitation (insufficiency): the valve leaflets fail to close in systole, so blood flows back from the left ventricle into the left atrium.
- Mitral valve prolapse: the leaflets bulge into the left atrium during systole. It is one of the commonest causes of regurgitation, along with rheumatic heart disease.

## Findings
- Most common symptoms: dyspnea, fatigue, weakness.
- Palpitations, exertional breathlessness and cough from pulmonary congestion.
- Murmur: high-pitched, blowing SYSTOLIC murmur at the apex.

## Management
- Afterload reduction (arterial dilation) helps, especially with heart failure: ACE inhibitors.
- Surgery: valve repair (valvuloplasty) or replacement.

## Nursing points
Assess for heart failure signs, teach to report worsening breathlessness or swelling, and see HF care in [[Left-Sided versus Right-Sided Heart Failure]].

## Compare stenosis and regurgitation
- Mitral stenosis: diastolic rumble (see [[Valvular Heart Disease: Overview and Mitral Stenosis]]).
- Mitral regurgitation: systolic blowing murmur.

## How the exam asks about it
- Murmur timing and quality questions. Memory trick (made up): regurgitation leaks, so it "blows".

## Related topics
[[Aortic Regurgitation]], [[Infective Endocarditis]]

title: Aortic Regurgitation
body:
## What it is
Aortic regurgitation (insufficiency): the aortic valve fails to close in diastole, so blood flows back from the aorta into the left ventricle.

## Causes
Inflammatory lesions deforming the leaflets, rheumatic endocarditis, congenital defects, syphilis, dissecting aneurysm; often idiopathic.

## Findings
- Forceful heartbeat felt in the head and neck; visible or palpable pulsations at the carotid or temporal arteries.
- Exertional dyspnea and fatigue.
- High-pitched, blowing DIASTOLIC murmur at the 3rd or 4th intercostal space, left sternal border.
- Widened pulse pressure and the water-hammer (Corrigan's) pulse, a sharp rise and quick collapse.

## Management
- Treatment of choice is aortic valvuloplasty or valve replacement, ideally before left ventricular failure develops; surgery is advised with left ventricular hypertrophy even without symptoms.
- Drugs: vasodilators (nifedipine), ACE inhibitors (captopril, enalapril, lisinopril, ramipril) or hydralazine.
- Advise avoiding physical exertion.

## How the exam asks about it
- Widened pulse pressure and water-hammer pulse point to aortic regurgitation.

## Related topics
[[Aortic Stenosis]], [[Mitral Regurgitation and Mitral Valve Prolapse]], [[Aneurysms]]

title: Aortic Stenosis
body:
## What it is
Narrowing of the opening between the left ventricle and aorta. The usual cause is degenerative calcification from years of normal mechanical stress and inflammation.

## Pathophysiology
As the opening narrows, the left ventricle pushes harder, uses more energy and compensates by thickening (hypertrophy). The thick muscle needs more oxygen but outflow to body and brain falls.

## Findings (the classic triad)
- Exertional dyspnea (raised pulmonary venous pressure) and possible pulmonary edema.
- Syncope and dizziness (less blood to the brain).
- Angina (high oxygen demand of the left ventricle).
- Loud, rough systolic murmur over the aortic area.
- Blood pressure may be normal.

## Treatment
Surgical aortic valve replacement or percutaneous valvuloplasty.

## Nursing points
Syncope risk means fall precautions; avoid heavy exertion; watch for angina and heart failure.

## How the exam asks about it
- Chest pain, fainting and breathlessness on exertion with a systolic ejection murmur at the aortic area.

## Related topics
[[Aortic Regurgitation]], [[Angina Pectoris: Types, Triggers and Findings]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout says BP is normal; many texts add a narrowed pulse pressure in severe stenosis.

title: Infective Endocarditis
body:
## What it is
A microbial infection of the heart's inner (endothelial) surface, usually in people with prosthetic valves or structural heart defects. Hospital-acquired cases follow indwelling catheters. Damaged endocardium collects fibrin and platelets (vegetations) and infection can erode into valves.

## Assessment findings
- Petechiae.
- Osler's nodes: small, PAINFUL nodules in finger or toe pads.
- Janeway lesions: flat, red-purple, PAINLESS macules on palms, fingers, toes.
- Roth spots: retinal hemorrhages with pale centers (from emboli).
- Splinter hemorrhages under nails.
- Fever and new or changing murmur are typical; emboli can travel (stroke, kidney).

## Treatment
- Long IV antibiotics, often a continuous infusion for 2 to 6 weeks; penicillin is usually the drug of choice. Fungal cases get an antifungal such as amphotericin B.
- Prevention: antibiotic prophylaxis for high-risk clients before dental procedures, tonsillectomy or adenoidectomy, bronchoscopy, cystoscopy, or surgery on infected skin or musculoskeletal tissue.

## Home teaching
- Aseptic technique for IV antibiotics; check the catheter site daily and report infection.
- Record temperature daily for up to 6 weeks and report fever.
- Oral hygiene twice daily with a soft toothbrush; avoid flossing and oral irrigators (they cause bacteremia).

## How the exam asks about it
- Match sign to name (painful Osler, painless Janeway). Also: which procedure needs prophylaxis.

## Related topics
[[Valvular Heart Disease: Overview and Mitral Stenosis]], [[Myocarditis]]

title: Myocarditis
body:
## What it is
Inflammation of the myocardium with cell injury and necrosis. Viral infection is the most common cause; bacteria, protozoa, fungi and parasites can also cause it. It is usually diagnosed when it impairs heart function.

## Findings
- Early: nonspecific fatigue, dyspnea, palpitations.
- Later: heart failure signs such as tachycardia, pulmonary edema, diaphoresis, neck vein distention, cardiomegaly.
- ECG: low-voltage QRS, ST elevation or heart block. S4 and systolic ejection murmur may be heard.
- Sudden cardiac death or rapid severe HF is possible.

## Management
- Treat the cause if known (for example penicillin for hemolytic streptococci).
- Inotropic support (dopamine, dobutamine); nitroprusside or nitroglycerin may reduce afterload.
- AVOID beta-blockers because they lower contractility (negative inotropes).
- Sedation and rest lower cardiac workload; an intra-aortic balloon pump or ventricular assist device may be used.

## Nursing alert
Clients with myocarditis are unusually sensitive to digitalis. Watch for toxicity: dysrhythmia, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, headache, malaise.

## How the exam asks about it
- Which drug should be avoided or monitored closely (beta-blockers avoided, digoxin toxicity).

## Related topics
[[Heart Failure: Types, Causes and Compensation]], [[Pericarditis and Pericardiocentesis]], [[ECG Waves and Intervals]]

title: Pericarditis and Pericardiocentesis
body:
## What it is
Inflammation of the pericardial sac. It may be a primary illness or arise during other medical or surgical conditions. It can lead to fluid accumulation (effusion) and [[Cardiac Tamponade]], or to scarring and a stiff pericardium that restricts filling (constrictive pericarditis), raising systemic venous pressure.

## Assessment
- Chest pain beneath the clavicle, in the neck or left scapular area; worse with deep inspiration, relieved by sitting and leaning forward.
- Hallmark sign: pericardial friction rub, creaky or scratchy, heard best at the left lower sternal border (4th intercostal space) with the diaphragm pressed firmly, louder at end-exhalation, best with the client sitting forward.

## Management
- Analgesics and NSAIDs. The handout says indomethacin is contraindicated because it may reduce coronary blood flow.
- Pericardial window (drainage into the chest cavity) or pericardiectomy for constriction.

## Pericardiocentesis (removing pericardial fluid)
- Have emergency resuscitation equipment ready; start a slow IV; raise the bed to 45 to 60 degrees; ultrasound guides the needle.
- Desired results: lower central venous pressure, rising blood pressure, disappearance of pulsus paradoxus and neck vein distention.
- Complications: coronary puncture, myocardial trauma, dysrhythmias, pleural laceration, gastric puncture.
- After: monitor rhythm, BP, venous pressure and heart sounds for return of tamponade.

## Nursing care
Pain control, positioning, emotional support; always be alert for tamponade.

## How the exam asks about it
- Pain that eases leaning forward plus a friction rub = pericarditis (not MI).

## Related topics
[[Myocardial Infarction: Presentation and Cardiac Markers]], [[Myocarditis]]

## Check against your textbook
- Indomethacin guidance is from the handout and differs from some references; verify.

title: Cardiac Tamponade
body:
## What it is
Fluid collecting in the pericardial sac squeezes the heart so it cannot fill, and cardiac output falls. A sudden build-up of just over 50 mL can cause acute tamponade.

## Causes
Cardiac trauma, complication of myocardial infarction, pericarditis.

## Findings
- Beck's triad: jugular vein distention, hypotension, muffled/distant heart sounds.
- Pulsus paradoxus: BP falls by more than 10 mm Hg on inspiration.
- Raised central venous pressure, low cardiac output, anxiety, dyspnea.
- Echocardiogram shows the fluid; chest X-ray also used.

## Priority nursing actions (unstable, so act fast)
1. Call for help; move or keep the client in a critical care unit for hemodynamic monitoring.
2. Give IV fluids as prescribed to support output.
3. Prepare for pericardiocentesis (see [[Pericarditis and Pericardiocentesis]]).
4. Monitor for recurrence after drainage.
5. Recurrent cases may need a pericardial window or pericardiectomy.

## Link to shock
Tamponade is a cause of cardiogenic shock: [[Circulatory Shock: Hypovolemic and Cardiogenic]].

## How the exam asks about it
- Falling BP with distended neck veins and quiet heart sounds after chest trauma or MI = tamponade; the action is prepare for pericardiocentesis and notify the provider.

## Memory aid
Beck's triad = "3 D's": Distended veins, Decreased BP, Distant heart sounds (made-up mnemonic).

title: Angina Pectoris: Types, Triggers and Findings
body:
## What it is
Episodes of chest pain or pressure from a mismatch: coronary blood flow is too low for the heart's oxygen demand. Usually due to atherosclerotic obstruction of at least one major coronary artery.

## Types
- Stable: predictable, on exertion, relieved by rest or nitroglycerin.
- Unstable (pre-infarction/crescendo): more frequent and severe, may not ease with rest or nitroglycerin. Treat as an emergency.
- Intractable/refractory: severe, disabling pain.
- Variant (Prinzmetal's): pain at rest with reversible ST elevation, from coronary spasm.
- Silent ischemia: ischemic changes without pain.

## Triggers
Exertion, cold, heavy meals (blood shunts to digestion), stress and strong emotion (catecholamines raise BP, heart rate and workload).

## Findings
- Heavy retrosternal pressure; radiation to neck, jaw, shoulders, inner upper arms (often left); apprehension, sense of doom.
- Hallmark: it subsides with rest or nitroglycerin.
- ECG may show ST depression or T-wave inversion; nuclear scans and angiography confirm.

## Priority nursing actions
Stop activity, sit/rest, check vital signs and give oxygen and nitroglycerin as ordered, get an ECG, and escalate if pain is not relieved (could be MI: [[Myocardial Infarction: Presentation and Cardiac Markers]]).

## How the exam asks about it
- Differentiate stable from unstable angina, and angina from MI (MI pain lasts longer than about 30 minutes and is not relieved by rest).

## Related topics
[[Angina Treatment: Procedures and Drugs]], [[Coronary Artery Disease and Atherosclerosis]]

title: Angina Treatment: Procedures and Drugs
body:
## What it is
Treatment aims to cut myocardial oxygen demand and raise supply.

## Procedures
- PTCA: balloon catheter opens a blocked vessel by compressing the plaque.
- Intracoronary stent: metal mesh scaffold that prevents sudden closure.
- Atherectomy: catheter with a cutting blade removes plaque.
- CABG: a graft vessel carries blood beyond the blockage.

## Drug classes
- Nitrates (nitroglycerin): dilate veins, so blood pools peripherally, less blood returns to the heart and workload falls. Forms: sublingual tablet, spray, topical, IV.
- Beta-blockers (metoprolol, atenolol): block beta stimulation of the heart, lowering oxygen use.
- Calcium channel blockers (amlodipine, diltiazem, felodipine): reduce workload; diltiazem is a main choice for vasospasm; useful if beta-blockers fail.
- Antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel; glycoprotein IIb/IIIa agents abciximab, tirofiban, eptifibatide): prevent platelet clumping.
- Anticoagulants (heparin, low-molecular-weight heparins enoxaparin, dalteparin): prevent clot formation.

## Nursing points
- Sit the client down before giving nitroglycerin (headache and hypotension are common).
- Monitor BP, pulse and pain relief; watch for bleeding with antiplatelets and anticoagulants.

## How the exam asks about it
- Which drug class acts by venous pooling (nitrates) and why they lower preload.

## Related topics
[[Angina Pectoris: Types, Triggers and Findings]], [[Myocardial Infarction: Management and Drug Therapy]], [[Coronary Artery Disease and Atherosclerosis]]

## Check against your textbook
- Nitroglycerin dosing, storage, and how many tablets to take before calling for help are not in the handout; confirm in your text.

title: Myocardial Infarction: Presentation and Cardiac Markers
body:
## What it is
In myocardial infarction (MI) part of the heart muscle is permanently destroyed, typically because a ruptured plaque forms a clot that completely blocks a coronary artery. The goal is to limit tissue death and prevent complications.

## Risk factors
- Non-modifiable: age, family history, ethnicity.
- Modifiable: hypertension, smoking, hyperlipidemia, obesity, diabetes, inactivity, stress.

## Presentation
- Severe chest pain usually longer than 30 minutes, radiating to left arm, back or jaw, often without a trigger and often in the morning; relieved only by opioids.
- Nausea, sweating, dyspnea, fear and anxiety, palpitations, fatigue.
- Cool clammy skin, S3 or S4, dysrhythmias, JVD if pump failure, crackles if congestion, pounding or thready pulse.

## Diagnostics
- ECG: T-wave changes, ST elevation, abnormal Q wave.
- Cardiac markers, in order of appearance:
  - Myoglobin: 1 to 3 hours, first to rise.
  - Troponin I: 2 to 4 hours, highly specific.
  - AST: about 8 hours (also liver).
  - CK-MB: about 24 hours; cardiac-specific.
  - LDH: about 72 hours.

## How the exam asks about it
- Order of markers; "which is the earliest?" (myoglobin), "which is most cardiac-specific?" (troponin, CK-MB).
- Chest pain priority: ECG, oxygen, notify provider. Compare [[Angina Pectoris: Types, Triggers and Findings]].

## Related topics
[[Myocardial Infarction: Management and Drug Therapy]], [[ECG Waves and Intervals]], [[Circulatory Shock: Hypovolemic and Cardiogenic]]

## Check against your textbook
- Marker timing differs slightly between sources; the handout's values are used here. Troponin timing is usually quoted as rising within a few hours.

title: Myocardial Infarction: Management and Drug Therapy
body:
## What it is
Management reopens the blocked artery and balances oxygen supply with demand.

## Goals
- Reperfuse the area (emergency thrombolytics or invasive procedures).
- Reduce oxygen demand and raise supply: oxygen, bed rest, drugs.

## Drugs
- Morphine IV: handout calls it the drug of choice; relieves pain, dilates vessels and lowers oxygen demand.
- Oxygen.
- Nitroglycerin: vasodilator.
- Aspirin (salicylate) and thienopyridine antiplatelets (clopidogrel, prasugrel); heparin as anticoagulant.
- Thrombolytics dissolve the clot so blood can flow again.
- ACE inhibitors (or ARBs) lower BP and workload.
- Beta-blockers (-olol).
- Statins (atorvastatin, rosuvastatin) lower cholesterol.
- Old shorthand is MONA (Morphine, Oxygen, Nitroglycerin, Aspirin); the handout's longer "THROMBINS2" mnemonic adds the rest.

## Priority nursing actions (ABCs and time-critical)
1. Assess ABCs, give oxygen, attach cardiac monitor, 12-lead ECG.
2. Establish IV access, give aspirin/nitroglycerin/morphine as ordered.
3. Prepare for reperfusion; "time is muscle".
4. Monitor for dysrhythmias, pump failure, bleeding after thrombolytics.
5. Keep the client on bed rest and calm.

## How the exam asks about it
- Immediate action for suspected MI, and which finding after thrombolytics must be reported (bleeding).

## Related topics
[[Myocardial Infarction: Presentation and Cardiac Markers]], [[Angina Treatment: Procedures and Drugs]], [[Cardiac Arrest and Basic Life Support Principles]]

## Check against your textbook
- Modern guidelines treat morphine and oxygen more selectively than the older MONA approach (oxygen mainly when saturation is low). Verify with your text. The handout's spelling "prasurgel" is prasugrel.

title: Cardiomyopathies: Dilated, Hypertrophic and Restrictive
body:
## What it is
Cardiomyopathy is a disease of the heart muscle with cardiac dysfunction. Three types.

## Dilated
- Damage to muscle fibres; both ventricles dilate with normal wall thickness and weak systolic function, so output falls.
- Causes: alcohol abuse, chemotherapy.
- Findings: fatigue, weakness, left-sided HF, dysrhythmias, moderate to severe cardiomegaly, exertional dyspnea, palpitations.

## Hypertrophic
- Asymmetric thickening of the ventricle, stiff LV with poor filling, and obstructed outflow. About half are inherited.
- Findings: dyspnea, angina, fatigue, syncope, palpitations, mild cardiomegaly, ventricular dysrhythmias, heart failure; sudden death is common.

## Restrictive
- Rigid, fibrosed walls cannot expand or contract; chambers narrowed; cause often unknown. Looks like constrictive pericarditis.
- Findings: dyspnea, fatigue, right-sided HF, mild to moderate cardiomegaly, heart block.

## Nursing focus
Treat as heart failure ([[Heart Failure: Types, Causes and Compensation]]), teach alcohol avoidance, monitor rhythm, and teach energy conservation.

## How the exam asks about it
- Match type to feature: alcohol = dilated; inherited with syncope and sudden death = hypertrophic; right HF with stiff walls = restrictive.

## Related topics
[[Left-Sided versus Right-Sided Heart Failure]], [[Pericarditis and Pericardiocentesis]]

title: Circulatory Shock: Hypovolemic and Cardiogenic
body:
## What it is
Shock is inadequate organ perfusion for the tissues' oxygen needs; hypoperfusion can exist even without marked hypotension. Three groups: hypovolemic, cardiogenic and distributive (see [[Distributive Shock: Neurogenic, Anaphylactic and Septic]]).

## Hypovolemic shock
- Fluid (blood or plasma) is lost: hemorrhage, severe vomiting or diarrhea, dehydration, burns or fistulas, massive third spacing.
- Treatment: stop or treat the cause and replace volume with blood, plasma, fluids and electrolytes.
- Goal: restore intravascular volume, redistribute fluid and correct the cause as fast as possible.

## Cardiogenic shock
- The pump fails: heart failure, MI, cardiac tamponade.
- Treatment: limit further heart damage, protect healthy muscle, and improve function by raising contractility and/or lowering afterload.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Airway, breathing, oxygen.
2. Control visible bleeding (hypovolemic); IV access.
3. Monitor BP, pulse, urine output, level of consciousness, skin.
4. In cardiogenic shock, be careful with big fluid volumes (lungs already congested) and follow orders.

## How the exam asks about it
- Identify type from the cause; recognise early signs (anxiety, restlessness, tachycardia) before BP drops.

## Related topics
[[Types of Shock]], [[Management of Shock]], [[Circulation and Shock Overview]], [[Cardiac Tamponade]]

title: Distributive Shock: Neurogenic, Anaphylactic and Septic
body:
## What it is
In distributive shock, widespread vasodilation lowers blood pressure and tissue perfusion even though blood volume may be normal.

## Neurogenic
- Loss of autonomic (sympathetic) tone below a spinal cord lesion causes rapid vasodilation and pooling of blood in peripheral vessels.
- Treatment restores sympathetic tone: stabilise the spinal injury and position properly.
- To avoid it with spinal or epidural anesthesia, keep the head of the bed raised at least 30 degrees so the anesthetic does not spread upward.

## Anaphylactic
- Allergic reaction releases histamine, causing systemic vasodilation.
- Remove the trigger (stop the drug), support airway and breathing, give epinephrine (vasoconstriction; emergency drug) and diphenhydramine (blocks histamine, reduces capillary leak).

## Septic
- Body reaction to bacterial toxins (often gram-negative) leaks plasma into tissues.
- Find and eliminate the infection.

## Summary of mechanisms
- Hypovolemic: lost volume. Cardiogenic: weak pump. Neurogenic: lost vasomotor tone. Anaphylactic: allergy. Septic: infection.

## Priority nursing actions
Airway first (anaphylaxis can close the airway), then oxygen, IV access, epinephrine as ordered, monitor vital signs.

## How the exam asks about it
- First action for a client who develops hives and wheeze after an antibiotic: stop the drug, check airway, call for help.

## Related topics
[[Circulatory Shock: Hypovolemic and Cardiogenic]], [[Sepsis and Septic Shock Recognition]], [[Types of Shock]]

title: Hypertension: Classification and Risk Factors
body:
## What it is
The handout defines hypertension as systolic BP above 140 mm Hg and diastolic above 90 mm Hg.

## Types
- Essential (primary): no known direct cause. Risk factors: age over 60, family history, excess calories, inactivity, heavy alcohol use, hyperlipidemia, high salt or caffeine, low potassium/calcium/magnesium intake, smoking.
- Secondary: caused by another disease, such as renal vascular or parenchymal disease, primary aldosteronism, pheochromocytoma, Cushing's disease, coarctation of the aorta, brain tumors, encephalitis.

## Nursing goals
Lower and control BP without side effects or unnecessary cost by:
- Adhering to the treatment plan.
- Making lifestyle changes (weight, salt, alcohol, smoking, exercise).
- Taking drugs as prescribed.
- Keeping follow-up appointments.

## Teaching points
Hypertension is often silent, so clients stop drugs when they feel well; stress that medicines are lifelong unless the provider changes them, and rise slowly from lying or sitting (orthostatic hypotension).

## How the exam asks about it
- Which risk factor is modifiable; which sign suggests secondary hypertension in a young person.

## Related topics
[[Antihypertensive Drug Classes]], [[Coronary Artery Disease and Atherosclerosis]], [[Aneurysms]]

## Check against your textbook
- Many current guidelines (for example ACC/AHA) use 130/80 as the threshold. Know your exam's reference value.

title: Antihypertensive Drug Classes
body:
## What it is
For uncomplicated hypertension without another indication, the handout lists diuretics, beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors as initial choices.

## Classes
- Beta-blockers: lower BP by reducing cardiac output, decreasing sympathetic stimulation and inhibiting renin release.
- ACE inhibitors (captopril, enalapril, lisinopril): reduce peripheral resistance without raising CO, HR or contractility; decrease aldosterone.
- Central alpha agonist (clonidine): acts on the CNS to reduce sympathetic outflow; does not reduce renal blood flow.
- Calcium channel blockers (verapamil, amlodipine, diltiazem, nicardipine).
- Diuretics: thiazide (chlorothiazide, hydrochlorothiazide), loop (furosemide, bumetanide), potassium-sparing (spironolactone).

## Nursing points
- Check BP and pulse before giving; hold and report per order or policy.
- Diuretics and electrolytes: monitor potassium (loop and thiazide lower it; spironolactone raises it).
- Teach slow position changes, daily weight if on diuretics, and not to stop abruptly (especially beta-blockers and clonidine).
- Encourage lifestyle measures along with drugs.

## How the exam asks about it
- Match class to action; or which lab to watch with each diuretic.

## Related topics
[[Hypertension: Classification and Risk Factors]], [[Drugs Used in Heart Failure]], [[Essential Drugs]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout calls beta-blockers "first line"; modern guidance generally favours ACE inhibitors/ARBs, calcium channel blockers or thiazides first. The handout also lists "central alpha antagonist"; clonidine is a central alpha-2 agonist. Verify.

title: Buerger's Disease (Thromboangiitis Obliterans)
body:
## What it is
Recurring inflammation of small and medium arteries and veins of the arms and legs. It is tightly linked to heavy smoking and chewing tobacco and typically affects men aged 20 to 35.

## Findings
- Cramping in the foot arch (instep claudication) after exercise; relieved by rest.
- Intense rubor (reddish-blue discoloration) of the foot and absent pedal pulses.

## Management
- Improve circulation to the limbs and stop disease progression. The key is complete nicotine cessation.
- Vasodilators are rarely prescribed.

## Nursing focus
- Stop all tobacco (see [[Stop Smoking and Tobacco Cessation]]).
- Protect the feet: warmth, proper footwear, avoid injury, inspect skin daily.

## How the exam asks about it
- Young male smoker with foot cramps relieved by rest and absent pedal pulses = Buerger's disease. Compare with [[Raynaud's Phenomenon]].

## Related topics
[[Deep Vein Thrombosis]], [[Coronary Artery Disease and Atherosclerosis]]

title: Raynaud's Phenomenon
body:
## What it is
Intermittent arteriolar vasoconstriction of the fingertips or toes that causes coldness, pain and pallor. Most common in women 16 to 40, more frequent in cold climates.

## Findings
- Typical color sequence: white (pallor), blue (cyanosis), then red (reactive flow).
- Numbness, tingling and burning pain as colors change.
- Usually bilateral and symmetric.

## Management
- Avoid triggers: cold and tobacco.
- Calcium channel blockers (nifedipine, amlodipine).
- Sympathectomy (interrupting sympathetic nerves) helps some clients.

## Nursing teaching
- Limit cold exposure; wear gloves, warm layers, and bring a sweater into air-conditioned rooms.
- Avoid smoking and all nicotine sources (gum, patches).

## How the exam asks about it
- Pick the right color sequence or the most important teaching (avoid cold and nicotine).

## Memory aid
White, Blue, Red = "WBR" (made-up). Compare with [[Buerger's Disease (Thromboangiitis Obliterans)]].

## Related topics
[[Stop Smoking and Tobacco Cessation]]

title: Deep Vein Thrombosis
body:
## What it is
A blood clot in a deep vein, usually of the leg. Virchow's triad explains why: vessel wall injury, venous stasis and altered coagulation. Stasis risks: bed rest, obesity, varicose veins, spinal cord injury, age over 65.

## Findings
Swelling of the limb (outflow blocked), pain, heaviness, ankle engorgement, edema, reduced function.

## Prevention
- Graduated compression stockings.
- Subcutaneous heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin for surgical clients.
- Weight loss, quitting smoking, regular exercise.

## Treatment
- Anticoagulants: heparin first, warfarin orally long term; thrombolytics (alteplase, urokinase, streptokinase) in selected cases.
- Monitor aPTT with heparin; PT and INR with warfarin.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Do not massage the leg (a clot could break off and travel to the lungs: [[Pulmonary Embolism]]).
2. Elevate the leg, give analgesics, apply warm moist packs.
3. Monitor clotting tests and watch for bleeding.
4. Walk once anticoagulated; avoid long sitting or standing.

## Stocking tip
For ambulatory clients, remove stockings at night and put them on before the legs touch the floor in the morning.

## How the exam asks about it
- Which lab for warfarin (INR/PT) vs heparin (aPTT); what sign suggests the clot has moved (sudden dyspnea, chest pain).

## Related topics
[[Pulmonary Embolism]], [[Buerger's Disease (Thromboangiitis Obliterans)]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout says to apply warm moist packs; some references limit local heat. Follow your text.

title: Aneurysms
body:
## What it is
A localized sac or dilation at a weak point in an artery wall.

## Causes
Congenital connective tissue disease (Marfan's), mechanical/hemodynamic (post-stenotic, arteriovenous fistula, amputation-related), trauma (pseudoaneurysm), infection (mycotic), pregnancy-related changes, inflammation, and graft or anastomosis failure.

## Types
- True aneurysm: one, two or all three layers of the artery are involved.
- False aneurysm: a pulsating hematoma; clot and connective tissue lie outside the arterial wall.
- Fusiform: symmetric spindle-shaped swelling of the whole circumference.
- Saccular: bulge on one side of the wall.
- Dissecting: a hematoma that splits the layers of the wall.

## Management
- Medical: keep BP controlled to prevent rupture using diuretics, beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, ARBs or calcium channel blockers.
- Surgical: resection with bypass graft, or endovascular stent-graft placed across the aneurysm.

## Nursing focus
Monitor BP, teach to report sudden severe pain (rupture or dissection), and avoid straining.

## How the exam asks about it
- Match the shape to the name; identify the BP goal.

## Related topics
[[Hypertension: Classification and Risk Factors]], [[Antihypertensive Drug Classes]], [[Aortic Regurgitation]]

title: Respiratory Anatomy and Control of Breathing
body:
## What it is
The respiratory tract has an upper part (nose, sinuses, pharynx, larynx, trachea) that filters, warms and moistens air, and a lower part (lungs, pleura, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli) that exchanges gas to regulate PaO2, PaCO2 and pH.

## Must-know facts
- Nose: passageway that filters, humidifies and warms air.
- Paranasal sinuses: resonating chambers for speech.
- Pharynx: tube joining nasal and oral cavities to the larynx.
- Larynx: the voice organ, joining pharynx and trachea.
- Trachea (windpipe): passage between larynx and bronchi.
- Lungs sit in the airtight thoracic cage; the pleura is the serous membrane lining the lungs and chest wall.
- Alveoli are the basic gas-exchange unit; oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the alveolar-capillary membrane by diffusion.

## Control of breathing
- Neural control is in the medulla, stimulated mainly by the carbon dioxide level in the blood.
- Chemoreceptors in the carotid arteries and aortic arch are a secondary system that respond to low oxygen (hypoxemia) and also stimulate the medulla.
- Alveolar stretch receptors signal the brain stem to stop inspiration and prevent over-distention.

## Why it matters
- This explains why high oxygen can suppress breathing in chronic CO2 retainers: see [[COPD Management and Nursing Care]].

## How the exam asks about it
- "What is the main stimulus to breathe in a healthy person?" (rising CO2).

## Related topics
[[Rhinitis: Allergic and Viral]], [[Breathing Assessment in the Primary Survey]]

title: Rhinitis: Allergic and Viral
body:
## What it is
Rhinitis is inflammation and irritation of the nasal mucosa.

## Allergic rhinitis
- Seasonal (pollen seasons) or perennial (year-round); triggered by dust, dander, pollens in sensitized people.
- Findings: runny nose (rhinorrhea), congestion, sneezing, itching of nose, palate, throat, eyes and ears.
- Treatment: antihistamines, nasal corticosteroid sprays, desensitization.
- Nursing: teach to avoid or reduce allergens and irritants; teach correct nasal drug use, and blow the nose first for best effect.

## Viral rhinitis (common cold)
- The most frequent viral infection; the handout names coronavirus as the cause.
- Highly contagious: the virus is shed for about 2 days before symptoms and early in illness.
- Findings: low-grade fever, congestion, rhinorrhea, sneezing, watery eyes, scratchy sore throat, malaise, chills, headache, muscle aches.
- Care is symptomatic: fluids, rest, avoid chilling, warm salt-water gargles, NSAIDs for aches, antihistamines for sneezing/runny nose, steam or humidified air.
- Antibiotics do not treat viral colds.

## How the exam asks about it
- Teaching: hand hygiene, covering the cough, and why antibiotics are not used.

## Related topics
[[Pharyngitis: Acute and Chronic]], [[Laryngitis]]

## Check against your textbook
- Rhinoviruses cause most colds; coronaviruses are one of several causes. Verify.

title: Pharyngitis: Acute and Chronic
body:
## What it is
Pharyngitis is inflammation of the pharynx, commonly called a sore throat.

## Acute
- Sudden painful inflammation of the back of the throat including the posterior tongue, soft palate and tonsils.
- Findings: fiery-red pharyngeal membrane and tonsils, swollen lymphoid follicles, tender cervical nodes, fever, malaise, sore throat.
- Drugs: penicillin is the treatment of choice; cephalosporins or macrolides as alternatives; benzocaine gargles for relief.
- Nursing: liquid or soft diet, cool or warm fluids, frozen desserts, warm saline gargles, more fluids, ice collar, bed rest during fever, prevention teaching.

## Chronic
- Persistent inflammation, common in adults who work in dust, overuse the voice, have chronic cough, or use alcohol and tobacco.
- Types: hypertrophic (thick congested mucosa); atrophic (late stage, thin, whitish, shiny, wrinkled); granular ("clergyman's sore throat", swollen lymph follicles on the wall).
- Findings: constant irritation or fullness, mucus in the throat, difficulty swallowing.
- Management: decongestant sprays (ephedrine, phenylephrine), antihistamine-decongestants, acetaminophen.
- Nursing: avoid contact with others while febrile; avoid alcohol, tobacco, smoke, cold and pollutants.

## Why it matters
Untreated streptococcal throat infection can cause rheumatic fever and valve damage: [[Valvular Heart Disease: Overview and Mitral Stenosis]].

## How the exam asks about it
- First-line antibiotic: penicillin. Teach to finish the entire course.

## Related topics
[[Tonsillitis, Adenoiditis and Tonsillectomy Care]], [[Peritonsillar Abscess (Quinsy)]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout says "three types" but describes only two clearly plus granular; the third (atrophic) is the late form of hypertrophic.

title: Tonsillitis and Tonsillectomy: Respiratory View
body:
## What it is
Tonsils (each side of the oropharynx) and adenoids (pharyngeal tonsils on the nasopharynx wall) are lymphatic tissue. Acute infection is usually from group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus (GABHS).

## Findings
- Sore throat, fever, snoring, difficulty swallowing.
- Enlarged adenoids: mouth breathing, earache, draining ears, frequent colds, bronchitis, foul breath, voice change, noisy breathing.

## Management
- Penicillin first line, or cephalosporins.
- Tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy if repeated infections despite antibiotics.

## Post-operative priorities (airway and bleeding first)
1. Position: prone or side-lying with the head turned to the side so secretions drain from mouth and throat.
2. Watch for hemorrhage: frequent swallowing is a red flag (blood running down the throat), also restlessness and rising pulse.
3. Ice collar to the neck; ice chips allowed.
4. Discourage coughing, throat clearing and excess talking.
5. Soft, cool diet; milk products may be restricted since they thicken mucus; avoid red-colored or hot foods and straws as ordered.
6. Alkaline mouthwash or warm saline for thick mucus and halitosis; cool-mist humidifier at home.
7. Avoid vigorous tooth brushing or gargling; avoid smoking and heavy exertion for 10 days.

## How the exam asks about it
- Which finding after tonsillectomy needs immediate action: frequent swallowing or bright red bleeding.

## Related topics
[[Pharyngitis: Acute and Chronic]], [[Peritonsillar Abscess (Quinsy)]], [[Airway Obstruction and Choking]]

title: Peritonsillar Abscess (Quinsy)
body:
## What it is
A collection of pus between the tonsillar capsule and surrounding tissues including the soft palate. It is the most common major pus-forming complication of tonsillitis or sore throat, from local cellulitis that becomes an abscess.

## Findings
- Severe sore throat, fever, raspy voice.
- Trismus (cannot open mouth) and drooling.
- Odynophagia (painful swallowing) and dysphagia.
- Ear pain (otalgia), tender enlarged cervical nodes.
- Airway obstruction can occur.

## Management
- Antibiotics (penicillin), corticosteroids, and needle aspiration to drain the abscess.

## Priority nursing actions (airway first)
1. Monitor airway; be ready to assist with intubation, cricothyroidotomy or tracheotomy if obstructed.
2. Assist with needle aspiration.
3. After the procedure: gentle cool saline gargles, cool liquids.
4. Teach oral hygiene and stopping smoking.

## How the exam asks about it
- A client with a sore throat who cannot open the mouth and drools: assess and protect the airway first.

## Related topics
[[Tonsillitis, Adenoiditis and Tonsillectomy Care]], [[Airway Obstruction and Choking]]

title: Laryngitis
body:
## What it is
Inflammation of the larynx, often from voice abuse or exposure to dust, chemicals, smoke and pollutants. Viruses are the commonest cause; bacterial infection may follow.

## Findings
- Hoarseness is the first sign; may progress to aphonia (complete voice loss).
- Severe cough.
- Throat feels worse in the morning and better in a warmer climate.

## Management and nursing
- Rest the voice and avoid irritants including smoking.
- Cool steam or aerosol inhalation; more oral fluids.
- Antibacterial therapy if ordered; topical inhaled corticosteroids may be given.

## Red flag
Hoarseness lasting more than about 2 weeks needs evaluation for cancer: see [[Cancer of the Larynx and Laryngectomy]].

## How the exam asks about it
- The best teaching is voice rest, humidity and stopping smoking.

## Related topics
[[Rhinitis: Allergic and Viral]], [[Stop Smoking and Tobacco Cessation]]

title: Cancer of the Larynx and Laryngectomy
body:
## What it is
Most laryngeal tumors are squamous cell carcinoma, more common in men aged 60 to 70. Cigarette smoking and alcohol are linked.

## Findings
- Hoarseness for more than 2 weeks, persistent cough and sore throat.
- Dyspnea, dysphagia, pain radiating to the ear, burning in the throat.
- Weight loss, enlarged cervical nodes, unilateral nasal obstruction.

## Diagnostics
Direct laryngoscopy (with biopsy), virtual endoscopy, optical imaging, CT and MRI.

## Treatment
- Radiation, chemotherapy, surgery.
- Partial laryngectomy: removes part of the larynx with one vocal cord and the tumor; hoarse voice may result.
- Total laryngectomy: removes laryngeal structures (hyoid, epiglottis, cricoid cartilage, 2 or 3 tracheal rings); permanent loss of voice; complications include salivary leak, wound infection, stomal stenosis, dysphagia.

## Nursing priorities
1. Airway: keep suction at bedside.
2. Observe for hemorrhage and infection.
3. Before surgery: establish a method of communication (writing board, picture board); arrange a visit from a support group.
4. Teach tracheostomy and stoma care.
5. Support grieving over loss of voice.

## How the exam asks about it
- The main pre-op teaching point is setting up a communication method; the first post-op priority is airway.

## Related topics
[[Laryngitis]], [[Stop Smoking and Tobacco Cessation]]

title: COPD: Chronic Bronchitis and Emphysema
body:
## What it is
COPD is airflow limitation that is not fully reversible, usually progressive, with an inflammatory lung response to irritants (smoking). It includes chronic bronchitis and emphysema.

## Chronic bronchitis ("blue bloater")
- Chronic inflammation with excess mucus; defined by productive cough for at least 3 months a year for 2 consecutive years.
- Thick, gelatinous sputum, more with infection; wheeze and dyspnea as disease progresses; insidious onset.

## Emphysema ("pink puffer")
- Destruction of alveolar walls and enlarged air spaces; slow decline over years.
- Panlobular type: whole lobule affected, hyperinflated chest, marked exertional dyspnea, weight loss.
- Centrilobular type: damage in the center of the lobule; V/Q mismatch gives chronic hypoxemia, hypercapnia, polycythemia, right-sided heart failure, central cyanosis.
- Findings: dyspnea, reduced exercise tolerance, minimal cough, barrel chest (increased anteroposterior diameter from air trapping and flat diaphragm).

## Diagnostics
- Spirometry shows airflow obstruction.
- ABG: low PaO2 and pH, raised CO2.
- Chest X-ray late: hyperinflation, flat diaphragm, widened retrosternal space, fewer vascular markings, bullae.
- Alpha-1-antitrypsin assay identifies the inherited deficiency.

## How the exam asks about it
- Identify type from appearance: blue bloater (cyanotic, edematous, productive cough) vs pink puffer (thin, breathless, barrel chest).

## Related topics
[[COPD Management and Nursing Care]], [[Bronchial Asthma]], [[Respiratory Failure Recognition]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout's panlobular details ("negative pressure required during inspiration") are unclear; confirm. Many texts attribute the "blue bloater" label more to bronchitis and "pink puffer" to emphysema, as given here.

title: COPD Management and Nursing Care
body:
## What it is
Care aims to slow progression, relieve symptoms and keep the client active.

## Medical and surgical management
- Smoking cessation (most important), bronchodilators, inhaled and systemic corticosteroids, alpha-1-antitrypsin augmentation, antibiotics, mucolytics, antitussives.
- Bullectomy: removes large non-functioning air spaces.
- Lung volume reduction surgery: removes diseased lung tissue.

## Priority nursing actions (breathing first)
1. Monitor respiratory rate and pattern, breath sounds, signs of distress.
2. Give LOW-flow oxygen (1 to 2 L/min): in chronic CO2 retainers, high oxygen can remove the hypoxic drive and depress breathing.
3. Give bronchodilators as prescribed; hydrate to thin secretions.
4. Teach pursed-lip breathing (slows expiration, keeps small airways open) and diaphragmatic breathing coordinated with activity.
5. Chest physiotherapy morning and night if ordered.
6. Small frequent meals and nutritional supplements to counter weight loss.
7. Alternate activity with rest; teach relaxation; avoid bronchial irritants.
8. Refer to pulmonary rehabilitation.

## How the exam asks about it
- Oxygen flow for COPD; best breathing technique; position (upright, leaning forward).

## Related topics
[[COPD: Chronic Bronchitis and Emphysema]], [[Stop Smoking and Tobacco Cessation]], [[Nutrition]]

title: Bronchial Asthma
body:
## What it is
A chronic inflammatory airway disease with hyperresponsiveness, mucosal swelling and mucus; narrowing is reversible and widespread.

## Findings
- Triad: cough, dyspnea, wheezing.
- Chest tightness, sweating, fast heart rate, widened pulse pressure, low oxygen, central cyanosis in severe attacks.
- A silent chest (no wheeze) in a distressed client is an ominous sign (made-up emphasis; not in handout).

## Drugs
- Quick relief: short-acting beta2 agonists (albuterol, levalbuterol, pirbuterol).
- Long-term control: corticosteroids, long-acting beta2 agonists, leukotriene modifiers (montelukast, zafirlukast, zileuton).

## Priority nursing actions
1. Assess severity: symptoms, breath sounds, peak flow, pulse oximetry, vital signs.
2. Give the quick-relief bronchodilator and oxygen as ordered; position upright.
3. Monitor response to drugs.
4. Hydrate if dehydrated.
5. Teach adherence, trigger avoidance and follow-up.

## How the exam asks about it
- Differentiate rescue from controller drugs; which assessment shows the attack is improving (better peak flow).

## Related topics
[[COPD: Chronic Bronchitis and Emphysema]], [[Respiratory Failure Recognition]]

title: Bronchiectasis
body:
## What it is
Chronic, irreversible widening of the bronchi and bronchioles.

## Causes
Airway obstruction, diffuse airway injury, severe or repeated pulmonary infections, genetic disorders such as cystic fibrosis, abnormal host defense (ciliary dyskinesia, immune deficiency), or unknown causes.

## Findings
- Chronic cough with large amounts of pus-like sputum.
- Hemoptysis, finger clubbing, repeated lung infections.
- CT scan shows the dilated bronchi.

## Management
- Smoking cessation, chest physiotherapy, bronchoscopy to remove secretions.
- Antibiotics guided by sputum culture and sensitivity.
- Influenza and pneumococcal vaccines; bronchodilators.
- Surgery if heavy sputum and bleeding persist despite treatment.

## Nursing actions
- Help clear secretions; teach postural drainage to client and family.
- Avoid people with respiratory infections.
- Encourage no smoking and good nutrition.

## How the exam asks about it
- Large daily volume of foul sputum plus clubbing = bronchiectasis. Compare [[COPD: Chronic Bronchitis and Emphysema]].

## Related topics
[[Pneumonia]], [[Pulmonary Tuberculosis: Diagnosis and Classification]]

title: Occupational Lung Diseases: Asbestosis, Silicosis, Sarcoidosis
body:
## What it is
Lung scarring from breathed-in dusts, or granuloma formation.

## The conditions
- Asbestosis: diffuse interstitial fibrosis from asbestos dust; workers who make, cut or demolish asbestos materials. Progressive, irreversible exertional dyspnea and bibasal crackles.
- Silicosis: chronic fibrosis from silica dust; mining (gold, coal, tin, copper), stone cutting, quarrying, abrasives, ceramics, pottery, foundry work. Productive chronic cough.
- Sarcoidosis: granulomas (clumps of inflammatory cells) in many organs, mainly lungs; lymph node enlargement on chest X-ray.

## Management
- No specific cure; remove exposure and treat symptoms.
- Prophylactic isoniazid for silicosis clients with a positive tuberculin test (high TB risk).
- Asbestos-exposed clients should stop smoking and be watched for lung cancer (changing cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, melena).
- Bronchodilators if airway obstruction.

## Nursing actions
Oxygen, bronchodilator teaching, smoking cessation, pacing activity, and prevention education for healthy workers.

## How the exam asks about it
- Match the dust to the disease and the occupation; link silicosis to TB risk.

## Related topics
[[Pulmonary Tuberculosis: Diagnosis and Classification]], [[Anti-TB Drugs and Nursing Care]]

title: Pneumothorax: Types and Findings
body:
## What it is
Air in the pleural space because the pleura was breached, so the lung collapses.

## Types
- Simple/spontaneous: air enters through a ruptured bleb or bronchopleural fistula.
- Traumatic: from rib fracture, stab or gunshot wounds, or diaphragmatic tear.
- Open: a chest wall wound large enough for air to pass in and out with each breath ("sucking chest wound").
- Tension: air enters on inspiration but cannot leave; pressure builds, the lung collapses and the heart, great vessels and trachea shift toward the unaffected side (mediastinal shift). A life-threatening emergency.

## Findings
- Hyperresonance, diminished breath sounds, reduced movement on the affected side.
- Tension: tracheal deviation away from the injured side, air hunger, agitation, hypotension, cyanosis, heavy sweating.
- Spontaneous: mild to moderate dyspnea and chest discomfort.

## Why it matters
Tension pneumothorax threatens cardiovascular collapse, so it is treated before imaging: decompress immediately.

## How the exam asks about it
- Recognise tension (deviated trachea, shock) vs simple. Then see [[Pneumothorax: Management and Chest Tube Care]].

## Related topics
[[Hemothorax]], [[Breathing Assessment in the Primary Survey]], [[Primary vs Secondary Survey]]

title: Pneumothorax: Management and Chest Tube Care
body:
## What it is
Treatment re-expands the lung and restores ventilation.

## By type
- Spontaneous: if small in a healthy person, observe for spontaneous resolution; larger ones need needle aspiration or chest tube. Recurrent cases: pleurodesis or thoracotomy with resection of apical blebs.
- Tension: immediate decompression (needle thoracentesis or chest tube) to prevent cardiovascular collapse, then chest tube with underwater-seal drainage.
- Open: close the wound immediately with petroleum gauze/occlusive dressing; chest tube with water-seal drainage; surgery may be needed.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Airway, breathing, oxygen; monitor oximetry and ABGs.
2. Cover a sucking wound at once.
3. Assist with emergency thoracentesis or thoracostomy.
4. Upright position if condition allows (best lung expansion).
5. Keep chest tubes patent (no kinks, drainage below the chest, tubing unclamped unless ordered).
6. Splint the chest when turning or coughing; give pain medicine so the client can breathe deeply.

## How the exam asks about it
- First action for a stab wound with bubbling air: cover it. For tension signs: prepare for decompression and notify the provider.

## Related topics
[[Pneumothorax: Types and Findings]], [[Hemothorax]], [[Pleural Effusion]]

## Check against your textbook
- Size thresholds for observation (the handout says under 50%) vary; many texts use smaller cutoffs.
- The handout describes a Valsalva-type breath while applying the dressing. Common teaching is an occlusive dressing taped on three sides to allow air to escape. Verify which your exam favors.

title: Pleural Effusion
body:
## What it is
Fluid (transudate or exudate) collects in the pleural space. Usually secondary to another disease: heart failure, pulmonary infection, nephrotic syndrome, malignancy.

## Findings
Dyspnea, difficulty lying flat, cough, fever, chills, pleuritic chest pain.

## Diagnostics
CT scan, lateral decubitus X-ray.

## Management
- Treat the underlying disease.
- Thoracentesis or chest tube drainage.
- Pleurectomy for malignant effusion; pleuroperitoneal shunt drains fluid from the pleural space into the abdomen.

## Nursing actions
- Assist with thoracentesis (client upright, leaning forward on a table, still); record amount of fluid and send it to the laboratory.
- Give analgesics and antibiotics as ordered.
- Position for comfort and breathing.

## How the exam asks about it
- Dullness to percussion and absent breath sounds over the fluid, with dyspnea. After thoracentesis, monitor for pneumothorax and respiratory distress.

## Related topics
[[Empyema Thoracis]], [[Hemothorax]], [[Heart Failure: Types, Causes and Compensation]]

## Check against your textbook
- Positioning for thoracentesis and the post-procedure checks are standard textbook knowledge added here, not in the handout.

title: Hemothorax
body:
## What it is
Blood in the pleural space from penetrating or blunt chest trauma. It accompanies many chest injuries and can hide large blood loss.

## Findings
May be symptom-free, or the client may be dyspneic, apprehensive or in shock.

## Management
- Thoracentesis to aspirate blood, or chest tube insertion with a drainage system for complete, continuous removal of blood and air.
- Replace volume with IV fluids or blood products.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Airway, breathing, oxygen; monitor for shock.
2. Auscultate lungs and watch for relief of dyspnea.
3. Measure and record chest tube drainage; report sudden large output.
4. Replace volume as ordered.

## Link
Massive blood loss can lead to [[Circulatory Shock: Hypovolemic and Cardiogenic]].

## How the exam asks about it
- After chest trauma, falling BP and rising pulse with decreased breath sounds suggest bleeding into the chest.

## Related topics
[[Pneumothorax: Management and Chest Tube Care]], [[Pleural Effusion]]

title: Pleurisy (Pleuritis)
body:
## What it is
Inflammation of both pleural layers (parietal and visceral). It may accompany pneumonia, upper respiratory infection, TB or collagen disease. The inflamed surfaces rub together, giving sharp, knife-like pain worse on inspiration.

## Findings
- Pain on deep breath, cough or sneeze, limited to a specific area.
- Pleural friction rub on auscultation.

## Diagnostics
Chest X-ray, sputum analysis, thoracentesis, pleural biopsy.

## Management
- Treat the underlying cause.
- Heat or cold applications; indomethacin for pain; intercostal nerve block for severe pain.

## Nursing teaching
- Heat/cold application for relief.
- Lie on the affected side to splint the chest wall and reduce stretching of the pleura.
- Hold a pillow or hands against the ribs when coughing.

## How the exam asks about it
- Pain that worsens with breathing and a friction rub; compare with [[Pericarditis and Pericardiocentesis]] where pain is eased by leaning forward.

## Related topics
[[Pneumonia]], [[Pleural Effusion]]

title: Empyema Thoracis
body:
## What it is
Pus in the pleural space, a complication of bacterial pneumonia, lung abscess or chest trauma. The client is acutely ill with signs like an acute respiratory infection.

## Diagnosis and treatment
- Chest CT establishes the diagnosis.
- Goal: drain the pleural cavity.
  - Thoracentesis if fluid is thin.
  - Tube thoracostomy for loculated or complicated effusions.
  - Open chest drainage via thoracotomy to remove thickened pleura, pus and debris.
- Antibiotics are also given (standard care, not stated in the handout).

## Nursing actions
Care follows the drainage method used (chest tube care, dressing care, monitoring output and character). See [[Pneumothorax: Management and Chest Tube Care]].

## How the exam asks about it
- Empyema = pus; effusion = fluid; hemothorax = blood. Know which drainage suits which.

## Related topics
[[Pleural Effusion]], [[Pneumonia]]

## Check against your textbook
- Antibiotic therapy is added from general knowledge.

title: Pneumonia
body:
## What it is
Inflammation of the lung tissue caused by bacteria, mycobacteria, fungi or viruses.
- Community-acquired: occurs in the community or within 48 hours of admission.
- Hospital-acquired (nosocomial): starts more than 48 hours after admission.
- Aspiration pneumonia: from entry of substances into the lower airway.

## Findings
- Sudden high fever (38.3 to 40.5 C), productive cough with purulent or rusty blood-tinged sputum.
- Pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, fast breathing, grunting, nasal flaring, accessory muscle use.
- Rapid bounding pulse, orthopnea, sweating, poor appetite.

## Diagnostics
Chest X-ray (consolidation), sputum Gram stain and culture and sensitivity, blood culture for bacteremia.

## Treatment
- Antibiotic matched to the organism; the handout lists a macrolide (azithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin) for S. pneumoniae.
- Viral pneumonia: supportive. Oxygen for poor gas exchange.
- Complications: shock, respiratory failure, pleural effusion.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Oxygenation and semi-Fowler's position.
2. Collect sputum specimen BEFORE the first antibiotic dose.
3. Encourage coughing and deep breathing, splinting the chest; suction if needed.
4. Hydration 2 to 3 L/day to thin secretions.
5. Rest periods; nutritious fluids.
6. Teach covering the mouth when coughing; finish the whole 7 to 10 day course; improvement is expected within 48 to 72 hours.

## How the exam asks about it
- Culture before antibiotics; position for best expansion; signs of failing oxygenation.

## Related topics
[[Pulmonary Tuberculosis: Diagnosis and Classification]], [[Pleurisy (Pleuritis)]], [[Respiratory Failure Recognition]]

## Check against your textbook
- Drug choice depends on organism and local guidelines; the handout's list is brief.

title: Pulmonary Tuberculosis: Diagnosis and Classification
body:
## What it is
TB is an infection mainly of the lung tissue; it can spread to meninges, kidneys, bones and lymph nodes. The organism, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, is an acid-fast aerobic rod, slow-growing, sensitive to heat and ultraviolet light, and spread person to person by AIRBORNE transmission.

## Findings
- Fatigue, loss of appetite, weight loss, low-grade fever, night sweats.
- Cough starting slowly, becoming more frequent with mucoid or pus-like sputum.
- Hemoptysis, chest pain and dyspnea suggest extensive disease.

## Diagnosis
- Sputum smear and culture confirm TB.
- Chest X-ray shows extent.
- Tuberculin skin test (PPD/Mantoux) shows exposure, not necessarily active disease.

## Classification (handout)
- Class 0: no exposure, no infection.
- Class 1: exposure, no infection evidence.
- Class 2: latent infection, no disease (positive PPD).
- Class 3: active disease.
- Class 4: disease, not clinically active.
- Class 5: suspected, diagnosis pending.

## Nursing priority
Airborne precautions: negative-pressure room and a particulate (N95-type) respirator for staff, mask for the client during transport.

## How the exam asks about it
- Which test confirms (sputum); which precautions (airborne); what a positive PPD means.

## Related topics
[[Anti-TB Drugs and Nursing Care]], [[Expanded Program on Immunization]], [[BCG and Pentavalent Vaccine]], [[Occupational Lung Diseases: Asbestosis, Silicosis, Sarcoidosis]]

## Check against your textbook
- Airborne precaution details are added from standard textbooks. Philippine TB programs use their own case definitions; the class system here is the older American one.

title: Anti-TB Drugs and Nursing Care
body:
## What it is
Pulmonary TB is treated with several drugs together for a long time (handout: 6 to 12 months).

## Regimen from the handout
- Initial phase: isoniazid (INH), rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol daily for 8 weeks.
- Continuation phase: INH and rifampin for another 4 or 7 months.
- Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) is given with INH to prevent peripheral neuropathy.

## Main side effects
- INH: peripheral neuritis, raised liver enzymes, hepatitis, hypersensitivity.
- Rifampin: hepatitis, fever, nausea and vomiting; (orange-colored body fluids is standard teaching).
- Pyrazinamide: high uric acid, liver toxicity, rash, joint pain, GI upset.
- Ethambutol: optic neuritis (vision changes, color discrimination), rash.
- Handout doses: INH 5 mg/kg (max 300 mg); rifampin 10 mg/kg (max 600 mg); pyrazinamide 15 to 30 mg/kg (max 2 g); ethambutol 15 to 25 mg/kg.

## Nursing actions
- Take on an empty stomach or at least 1 hour before meals (food reduces absorption).
- Avoid tyramine- and histamine-rich foods with INH (headache, flushing, low BP, palpitations, sweating).
- Monitor for side effects, especially liver and vision.
- Stress completing the whole regimen: stopping early causes drug-resistant TB.
- Hygiene: cover the mouth when coughing, dispose of tissues, wash hands.
- Rest, fluids, small frequent nutritious meals.

## How the exam asks about it
- Match drug to adverse effect; what to teach about adherence.

## Related topics
[[Pulmonary Tuberculosis: Diagnosis and Classification]], [[Essential Drugs]], [[Treatment of CD, NCD and Emergency Services]]

## Check against your textbook
- Doses, the 8-week/4-7 month schedule and the food advice are from the handout and may differ from the DOH program. Verify before relying on them. Rifampin sometimes taken with food in practice if GI upset.

title: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)
body:
## What it is
A severe form of acute lung injury: sudden, progressive pulmonary edema with bilateral infiltrates on chest X-ray and hypoxemia that does not improve with oxygen, without raised left atrial pressure. Lung compliance falls.

## Findings
- Develops over about 4 to 48 hours.
- Severe dyspnea, labored fast breathing, severe hypoxemia unresponsive to oxygen.
- Crackles and rhonchi, increased alveolar dead space.
- X-ray looks like cardiogenic pulmonary edema.

## Diagnostics
History and presentation, ABG showing hypoxemia despite more oxygen, bilateral infiltrates, BNP and echocardiogram (to exclude heart failure), pulmonary artery catheter.

## Treatment
- Treat the cause; optimise oxygenation.
- Intubation and mechanical ventilation with PEEP, sedation, sometimes paralytics, antibiotics as indicated.
- Supportive: surfactant replacement and other drugs mentioned in the handout.

## Priority nursing actions
1. ICU monitoring, frequent reassessment.
2. Turn the client often to improve ventilation, perfusion and drainage.
3. Promote rest to cut oxygen demand.
4. Nutrition: 35 to 45 kcal/kg/day (handout).
5. Reassure; look for anxiety linked to ventilator problems.

## How the exam asks about it
- Hypoxemia not corrected by oxygen with bilateral white-out. See also [[Respiratory Failure Recognition]].

## Related topics
[[Pneumonia]], [[Sepsis and Septic Shock Recognition]], [[Pulmonary Embolism]]

## Check against your textbook
- Surfactant and "pulmonary antihypertensive" drugs are not standard in all references; verify.

title: Pulmonary Embolism
body:
## What it is
Blockage of the pulmonary artery or a branch by a clot, usually from a deep vein (see [[Deep Vein Thrombosis]]). Risks: trauma, surgery (orthopedic, abdominal, pelvic), pregnancy, heart failure, age over 50, clotting disorders, immobility.

## Findings
- Dyspnea (most common symptom) and tachypnea (most frequent sign).
- Sudden pleuritic chest pain that can mimic angina or MI.
- Anxiety, tachycardia, fever, cough, sweating, hemoptysis, syncope, petechiae over the chest.

## Diagnostics
- Pulmonary angiography (best method per the handout), V/Q scan, spiral CT.
- ABG: low oxygen and low CO2. ECG: sinus tachycardia, nonspecific T changes. Chest X-ray: infiltrates, atelectasis, raised diaphragm.

## Treatment
- Oxygen immediately, IV access, dobutamine or dopamine for hypotension, small doses of IV morphine for anxiety and chest pain.
- Anticoagulants (heparin, warfarin); thrombolytics (urokinase, streptokinase, alteplase) in severe cases; embolectomy for massive PE.

## Priority nursing actions (ABC)
1. Oxygen, raise the head of the bed, call the provider.
2. Monitor hypoxia, bleeding from anticoagulants, and signs of right ventricular failure or cardiogenic shock.
3. Prevent recurrence: early ambulation, leg exercises, avoid crossing legs, constrictive clothing and long sitting or bed rest.

## How the exam asks about it
- Sudden dyspnea and chest pain after surgery or long immobility. Compare with [[Myocardial Infarction: Presentation and Cardiac Markers]] and [[Angina Pectoris: Types, Triggers and Findings]].

## Related topics
[[Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)]], [[Respiratory Failure Recognition]], [[Cardiac Arrest and Basic Life Support Principles]]
